newsitem.title: USA: Dusting of snow protects HRW wheat, cold lingers.
newsitem.headline: Dusting of snow protects HRW wheat, cold lingers.

text.p: A dusting of snow overnight in the panhandle of Oklahoma and Texas eased concerns of winter kill in the dormant wheat crop, but below-normal temperatures were expected the rest of the week, meteorologists said.
Light snow was falling in western Kansas Tuesday morning and heavier snows were forecast for later in the day, said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.

"We expect to see a little bit heavier snow this afternoon and tonight in northwest Kansas and Nebraska," Burgio said. "If it comes over into the Midwest, it will pick up a bit of moisture and we could see three to six inches there."

"Below normal temperatures is going to be the rule east of the Rockies," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster with Weather Express. "We're looking at single digits to teens for lows for most mornings in the southern hard red (winter wheat) areas."
Gesser said a low pressure area was forming in Kansas and Nebraska on Tuesday and should move east, bringing two to four inches of snow to the Missouri Valley and Midwest.

The snow could further impede grain movement out of the U.S. Midwest. Cash grain dealers said farmers were actively selling soybeans after CBOT prices rallied more than 30 cents per bushel in two trading days.
But parts of the Illinois River were frozen north of Peoria and barges were not moving. Forecasters said there was little chance of a thaw this week.

Temperatures were expected to warm slightly on Wednesday because cloud cover offers some insulation, Gesser and Burgio said. Another cold front was forecast to move across the U.S. Plains and Midwest on Thursday and Friday but Gesser said the snow cover should protect dormant winter wheat crops.
"We're fairly well protected all across Kansas and even up into the Ohio Valley and Illinois," he said. "Your snow line now is quite a bit farther south than it was a week ago."
Long-range forecasts indicated a brief warm-up on Saturday, followed by another blast of cold air. ((Emily Kaiser 312-408-8749))
